Spain’s latest train crash likely dashes Sánchez’s reelection dream

Presented by European Commission’s Directorate-General for Research and Innovation By AITOR HERNÁNDEZ-MORALES with RAFAEL MÉNDEZ and VICTOR GOURY-LAFFONT PRESENTED BY Send tips here | Listen to Pla…

Actual Article Body:
Europe’s political and policy moves shaping tomorrow’s Brussels agenda.

				Privacy Policy and
				Terms of Service apply.

Presented by European Commission’s Directorate-General for Research and Innovation

By AITOR HERNÁNDEZ-MORALES

with RAFAEL MÉNDEZ and VICTOR GOURY-LAFFONT

PRESENTED BY

Send tips here | Listen to Playbook and view in your browser

BUENAS TARDES, Aitor Hernández-Morales here to bring you the latest on how today’s tragedy in Spain is turning political.

NO, CANADA: EU countries have dropped the idea of offering Canada “associate member” status in the 27-member bloc, opting instead for softer language promising “ever closer association.”

TRAIN CRASH LATEST: At least 68 people were killed and 58 injured when two trains collided near Madrid this morning, according to emergency services. Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by an official in the national railway control center in Madrid, who “inexplicably” instructed one high-speed train to proceed along a track where another had stalled.

“We are absolutely devastated,” said Puente, who has been touted as a possible future Socialist Party leader. “We have a safe rail system, comparable to those of other countries in our region.”

Puente declined to say whether he would resign over the tragedy.

**A message from the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Research and Innovation: Ekaterina Zaharieva: Europe has extraordinary talent and ideas. We need to help them go further. Join me at the European Research and Innovation Days on 10–11 November 2026 to discuss how we can connect researchers, innovators and entrepreneurs, support startups and turn discoveries into real benefits for people across Europe.**

GAME OVER? Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s chances of victory in next month’s parliamentary elections already looked like a long shot before today’s train accident. The dream that he’ll be able to continue as PM now looks very unlikely to come true given the Socialist leader’s checkered record on crisis management and improving public services.

Déjà vu: The crash comes less than a year after a train derailment in Adamuz killed 46 people. This raises major questions about the state of Spain’s critical infrastructure and threatens Sánchez’s central pitch to voters: that his government is competent and bettering Spaniards’ everyday lives.

Give it to us straight: “This inevitably upends the campaign and deals a blow to Sánchez,” said a Socialist Party lawmaker who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “It changes the conversation, and naturally the opposition will use it, just as they used the Adamuz accident.” Another anonymous Socialist lawmaker cautioned against writing Sánchez off, noting that a month remains until election day — a lifetime in politics.

Leadership scrutiny: Sánchez will very likely face fresh questions about his leadership. He’s already dealing with corruption scandals involving close allies, and few have forgotten his missteps while handling the mass arrival of migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in July.

Adiós, charm offensive: Sánchez will also probably need to adjust his campaign strategy, at least in the short term. The PM had recently been playing up his charisma in contrast to dour, gaffe-prone rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo and doubling down on his bet to make the election about housing policy. Even Sánchez’s critics had started suggesting his Socialist Party could finish first in the popular vote — though still short of the parliamentary majority needed to govern given the disarray of his potential coalition partners on the left.

Vox doesn’t hold back: Feijóo’s center-right People’s Party, which leads in the polls, has so far limited its response to expressing solidarity with the victims and their families. Far-right Vox leader Santiago Abascal, however, slammed the government. “More deaths. Another tragedy. More anger at the abandonment, ruin and betrayal Spaniards are suffering,” he wrote on X. “I will not rest until this government, which is a criminal organization, is in the dock answering for its crimes.”

BAD TO WORSE: Pessimism is palpable among France’s flailing centrists as they brace for another weekend of protests over conditions in schools and the rising cost of living. “Honestly, I don’t know how we’re going to pull this off. Things are dragging on, and we’re out of ideas,” said one centrist MP granted anonymity to speak candidly.

We’re the problem: Another lawmaker said the government’s failure to stop the violence on the sidelines of the demonstrations that took place on Oct. 17 “is definitely going to kill us. We can no longer be a solution, only a problem.”

Who’s in, who’s out: There are less than six months before the first round of France’s next presidential election, and polls show far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen and far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon have the inside track to take the top two spots and advance to the runoff. Former PMs Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal as well as conservative leader Bruno Retailleau are all bleeding support.

Too many options: “There are too many [candidates],” said France’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot on public radio this morning, echoing calls for centrists, the center-right and conservatives to rally around a single candidate to avoid vote-splitting.

Foreign interference: Barrot and other centrists are trying to seize the narrative about the situation facing France. The FM used his interview to dispel unsubstantiated claims that the violence was linked to immigration, attributing those claims to “interference attempts” from countries including the U.S., Israel, Iran and Russia. But Philippe said in an interview that during the unrest an “overrepresentation of young people from immigrant backgrounds was evident.”

Commissioning a commission: National Assembly President Yaël Braun-Pivet has been attempting to put together a parliamentary commission to investigate the violence that took place over the weekend of Oct. 17 and 18, but even this effort looks imperiled by bickering over which lawmakers get key positions.

BRITISH BUDGET: Chancellor John Healey reduced his fiscal buffer and slapped fresh taxes on banks Wednesday as he announced the first government budget under PM Andy Burnham. Showing his boss is focused on the cost-of-living crisis, Healey promised a £100 energy payment for millions of Brits over the winter, while repeatedly pointing to the war in the Middle East as justification.

PAVLOVIAN RESPONSE: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s top pick for Ukrainian ambassador to the U.S. declined the job in favor of a return to the front line. According to Zelenskyy, former top military commander and current Deputy Head of the President’s Office Pavlo Palisa told his boss: “Get me back to my brigade immediately. I’m not leaving Ukraine.”

MAYDAY: Drones struck a container vessel off the coast of Bulgaria on Wednesday afternoon, said Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov. There is no information yet as to who is responsible, but concerns over attacks on civilian commercial vessels in the region are growing. Bulgaria is also seeking dedicated EU funding in the next long-term budget to help set up a planned Black Sea Maritime Security Hub with Romania.

HEADS UP: As tensions in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean rise, Turkish Defense Minister Yaşar Güler warned Tuesday that Ankara would not compromise on its rights and interests. He also stressed the importance of maintaining open channels of communication with Greece.

BILLET-DOUX: The mayor of Limoges, whose town hall was set ablaze during the unrest in France earlier this month, said this morning he had not been contacted by President Emmanuel Macron since the incident … but had received an e-mail from U.S. Vice President JD Vance, who has turned the unrest in France into a campaign issue ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

FORT TRUMP: Polish President Karol Nawrocki has summoned the country’s top security officials for a Nov. 3 meeting to discuss plans for a permanent U.S. military base, ahead of his meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump at December’s G20 summit in Miami. Dubbed “Fort Trump,” the prospective base would accommodate some 5,000 American troops and their families, at an estimated cost of €3.5 billion.

PATRIOT PRIZE: Poland beat Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host a European servicing center for U.S.-made PAC-3 missiles — the advanced Patriot interceptors used to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles in Ukraine. The facility will allow European militaries to service the sought-after weapons without sending them across the Atlantic.

LET’S TALK: The U.K. will kickstart negotiations with European allies over its joint procurement scheme for their defense industries, after talks collapsed over joining Canada’s defense bank. The Multilateral Defence Mechanism was announced by former PM Keir Starmer’s government in March alongside the Netherlands and Finland. Poland joined in July.

ON THE FENCE: Spain and Slovenia “have not yet decided” if they will compete in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest after boycotting this year’s event over Israel’s participation, the European Broadcasting Union said Wednesday. They have until December to decide. But Ireland, the Netherlands and Iceland will once again boycott the competition.

EXPECT: No planned works or delays on public transit as you head home this evening, according to STIB.

Today’s recommendations are:

READ THIS: “Days of Love and Rage,” an epic portrait of the city of Manbij during the Syrian civil war that took journalist Anand Gopal eight years to complete.

LISTEN TO THIS: A chronicle of What Went Wrong on the set of 1964’s “Dr. Strangelove” and the fear of nuclear war that inspired it.

WATCH THIS: Head to your preferred streamer for the movie that brought us the modern zombie, George A. Romero’s 1968 classic “Night of the Living Dead.”

LEFT IN THE LURCH? HEAD TO THIS: This year’s Pink Screens Film Festival kicks off with an exhibition and concert at LaVallée tonight. More info here.

IMO: The Oxford — or serial — comma serves a purpose and should not be optional punctuation. AP take note. — Leyla Aksu, deputy editor

TALK TO PLAYBOOK: Do you agree? Email us at [email protected] to share your Brussels takes.

TRAIN DREAMS: Spain came to Europe’s high-speed rail revolution relatively late. Italy boasted the continent’s first line in 1977, France in 1981 and Germany a decade on. Spain joined the race in 1992, inaugurating its state-of-the-art AVE service between Madrid and Seville in time for the 500th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’ voyage to the Americas. Pursuing ambitious expansions, it now hosts Europe’s largest network — only China’s is larger. But the Adamuz disaster in January has caused a significant drop in ridership.

Our job is to help them succeed. On 10–11 November 2026, the European Research and Innovation Days will bring these communities together with policymakers and business leaders. We look forward to hearing their ideas on how we can make Europe a better place to do research, build a business and bring new technologies to market. Steering our discussions will be the European Research Area. How can we make it easier for people, knowledge and ideas to move across borders? Stated Claim / Post Context:
Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes | CNN

Scores of people have been killed and around 100 injured after two Spanish trains — carrying about 500 passengers — collided south of Madrid. Follow for live updates.

Actual Article Body:
Live Updates

• Deadly rail crash: Scores of people have been killed and about 100 injured after a high-speed train collided with a stationary train. Spain’s transport minister called it “inexplicable” that a train was allowed to continue its journey despite a red signal being in place.

• ‘People were hurled into the air’: Several witnesses told CNN about the chaotic moment when passengers were thrown airborne during the collision. Rescue operations are still under and the high-speed line linking Madrid with Andalusia remains suspended.

• Third train crash this year: This is the third rail disaster in Spain in 2026. In January, two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz, in southern Spain’s Córdoba province, killing more than 40 people. A commuter train near Barcelona derailed days later.

• Sigue nuestra cobertura en vivo en español

After a host of European leaders offered their condolences for the victims of the deadly train crash in Spain this morning, other international leaders are also expressing their solidarity today.

An erroneous order from a train controller, following a signaling system failure, resulted in Wednesday’s deadly train crash, according to Spain’s transport minister.

Speaking during a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, Óscar Puente said that a computer failure with the main LZB signalling system triggered an automatic stop for all trains in that area, including the Renfe high-speed train and Iryo train involved in the collision.

The control system for Adif, Spain’s railway infrastructure manager, then took command of the system and a decision was made for the Renfe train to continue its journey and the train was authorized to proceed despite a red signal prohibiting movement remaining in place.

The Iryo train remained stationary on the track around 25 kilometers (16 miles) ahead.

The Renfe train was authorized to proceed without any speed restrictions, meaning that between 8:36 a.m. and 8:52 a.m. local time, it traveled approximately 25 kilometers (16 miles) at a speed of about 200 kilometers per hour (124 miles per hour) before colliding with the Iryo train, Puente said.

The transport minister described the crash as “truly implausible” and said that the control center’s decision to allow the Renfe train to resume its journey while the Iryo train was stopped on the track was “inexplicable.”

This post has been updated with additional reporting.

Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said authorities are working hard to identify the cause of today’s deadly train crash in Toledo province, and vowed that any negligence, if identified, will be addressed with “utmost firmness.”

“We are going to get to the bottom of it. And if there has been negligence, it will come to light. And if there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness. Because it is clear that we have suffered two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail in the same year,” he said at a news conference near the site of the crash.

Sánchez added that if Spain must “strengthen safety even further in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so. Because what is unacceptable for a country like Spain is to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have.”

“Therefore, every measure considered appropriate will be taken,” he said.

He also said the cause of the crash was “not for me to say,” but rather for the train network operators and the country’s Independent Commission on Rail Accidents to investigate.

Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is at the scene of the train collision, where he offered his condolences and announced three days of official mourning.

“Today, Spain is in mourning. All of Spain is in mourning,” he said, saying he expressed his “full solidarity” with victims’ families.

“Behind every person who has died today, there are shattered lives, there are broken families. There is also the anguish of those families who still do not know the whereabouts of their loved ones. And, of course, there is a great deal of pain, a great deal of pain that Spanish society as a whole naturally shares.”

At least 68 people have been killed and another 58 have been injured after two trains collided in the Spanish province of Toledo, local officials have said.

Here are some of the latest developments:

CNN’s Magdalena Sofia Vitores Moreno, Benjamin Brown, Sophie Tanno, Vasco Cotovio, Pau Mosquera and Lauren Kent contributed to this reporting.

Emergency crews are working at the site of a deadly train collision in Spain’s Toledo province today, in which at least 64 people were killed and dozens more injured.

Train passengers have told CNN that the moment of the crash was “very chaotic” and people were immediately thrown out of their seats and on top of one another inside the train carriages.

Authorities have moved at least one bus full of passengers who do not have serious injuries away from the site. Several passengers being bussed away had minor injuries, including cuts on their faces and around their eyes, and what appeared to be bloody noses. Many people also had blood on their hands and arms.

“There was terrible communication. No one could leave the trains for 10 minutes after the crash, we didn’t know what was happening,” said one passenger, Rey, who declined to give his last name.

He said he and his family, who were on the way to a vacation in Seville, are OK but also “desperate to go.” More busses have arrived on the scene now to move additional passengers away from the area.

Another passenger, Yoander, 25, told CNN: “I was sleeping, and when I woke up I was already crashing into the seats in front of me.”

“I hit my face and my leg,” he said. “I’m in pain, but there are people that need more help than I do.”

The deadly train crash in Spain’s Toledo province has some similarities with a train disaster in Córdoba province that killed more than 40 people earlier this year.

Both train collisions happened along the same high-speed rail route that runs between the capital, Madrid, and Seville, about 300 miles south.

The Toledo crash happened about 130 miles from the site of January’s train disaster near Adamuz, in Córdoba province. Following Wednesday’s crash, authorities have suspended that high-speed line linking the Madrid region with Andalusia.

Both train accidents also involved the collision of two high-speed trains, although one of the trains on Wednesday was not travelling at high speed at the time of the crash.

Spanish emergency authorities have not yet announced a precise cause of Wednesday’s crash, but they have disclosed some details. The local Castilla-La Mancha 112 emergency services told CNN they received a report of a collision at 8.45 a.m. local time. According to the reports, a train owned by the company Iryo was stationary or traveling at low speed when it was struck by a high-speed AVE train operated by Spain’s national railway company Renfe.

It appears the crash on Wednesday was a rear-end collision, authorities at the scene told CNN. The train crash earlier this year involved one train derailing and crossing onto an adjacent track, according to Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE.

For context: Spain’s train drivers’ union, Semaf, has previously raised concerns about high speeds causing vibrations and subsequent wear and tear along high-speed railway lines, a source from the union told CNN in January, in the aftermath of the crash near Adamuz.

In August 2025, the union sent a letter to the national railway operator, Adif, asking for a reduction in the maximum speed on all high-speed train lines from 300 kmph to 250 kmph, after some stretches were vibrating and placing stress on the infrastructure, the source said.

CNN’s Pau Mosquera, Tim Lister and Sophie Tanno contributed to this report.

Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will travel to Urda, the town closest to the site of the train crash, the country’s government said in a post on X.

While in Urda, Sanchez will  “back the works of the emergency teams and bring support to the affected and their families,” the government said.

“The priority is to tend to the victims and provide the best coordination among different administrations,” the social media post continued.

There has been an outpouring of grief from neighboring European leaders today, after two trains collided in the Spanish province of Toledo, killing dozens of people.

Leaders from the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Belgium, Germany, Ukraine, The Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, Norway, Finland, the Czech Republic, Lithuania, Latvia, Romania, Estonia, Croatia, North Macedonia, Slovakia, Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Andorra also expressed their sympathies.

CNN’s James Frater, Duarte Mendonça, Sharon Braithwaite and Magdalena Vitores Moreno contributed to this reporting.

Correction: An earlier version of this post misstated the title of French President Emmanuel Macron.

At least 64 people have now been confirmed killed in a deadly train collision in Spain this morning, a spokesperson for the regional Castilla-La Mancha government said.

The spokesperson told CNN that this number is expected to rise further as emergency workers continue to work at the scene.

The death toll from today’s train crash in the Spanish province of Toledo has now risen to at least 32, according to Emiliano García-Page, the president of the regional Castilla-La Mancha government.

García-Page shared the latest update when speaking to Spanish national broadcaster Radio Nacional de España.

Previously, authorities had said that at least 30 people had been killed and around 100 injured in the collision.

The Spanish Civil Guard announced that they have opened four offices in different cities of Spain in order to swiftly identify the victims of the crash.

A spokesperson of institution has said they will also take DNA samples of the relatives to bring a quick response. “We are calling all close relatives to get to this offices and speed up the identification process,” the spokesperson said.

The offices are in the Civil Guard zones of Madrid, Andalusia, Cordoba and Toledo.

CNN’s Pau Mosquera has been reporting from Urda, a town roughly five miles from the site of today’s deadly train crash.

Dozens of ambulances and emergency service vehicles have been streaming into the town’s sports centre, where Red Cross workers are treating the injured.

One of the survivors recounted how she was thrown from her seat as the crash’s impact sent her flying into the air. She was grateful for the care provided to her by the emergency staff in Urda.

The scene at the site of the crash is frantic as a serious rescue operation is underway, according to CNN’s team on the ground in Toledo province.

Dozens of fire trucks, ambulances and police cars are here. At least three helicopters are also at the crash site to assist with operations. Multiple ambulances have come and gone from the cordoned-off area.

Meanwhile, emergency responders are combing through the rubble of some of the heavily damaged carriages of the train operated by Iryo. Several carriages of the state-owned Renfe high-speed train are tilted on their side after coming off the rails.

The Spanish civil guard has set up multiple tents for what amounts to a huge emergency response.

Authorities have moved a bus full of passengers who do not have serious injuries away from the site, and some those passengers told CNN they are now being taken to their original destination of Sevilla.

Passengers described a chaotic scene when their train hit another train on the tracks.

Those being bussed away from the crash site included citizens of multiple nationalities, including Spain, Brazil and elsewhere. Staff from the US Embassy in Spain are also at the site.

A woman traveling on one of the trains involved in a deadly collision Wednesday morning has described “awful” scenes as people were thrown into the air.

Patricia was sitting in the third carriage of the AVE high speed train, operated by Renfe, Spain’s national railway company, when it collided with a train owned by the company Iryo.

Speaking to CNN, Patricia told how her train had been stopped for around 20 minutes before the accident, with an announcement explaining there was a lot of traffic. “After that we departed, and maybe not after even three minutes, there was a crash,” she said.

Patricia said the crash seemed to last a long time.

“Some people were hurled into the air. Not me. I was on the left side so I suppose that’s why I wasn’t hurled in the air, but it was awful.”She continued, “Some of the train structure got into our train, in our carriage, and our carriage wasn’t even the worst.”

The Castilla-La Mancha regional government has called for blood donations following today’s train crash.

“Donate blood,” reads a post on X. “Today your solidarity is very important.”

The post calls for donations in Alcázar de San Juan, Ciudad Real and Toledo.

At least 30 people have been killed and around a hundred injured in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo this morning, according to a local government official and emergency services. The incident is the third rail disaster in Spain this year.

Here’s what we know about the deadly collision so far:

CNN’s Pau Mosquera, Sophie Tanno, Magdalena Sofia Vitores Moreno and Lauren Kent contributed to this reporting.

At least 30 people have been killed after two trains collided in Spain this morning, according to a local government official.

The spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government told CNN that the death toll is likely to rise.

This post has been updated with additional developments.

Today’s train crash occurred in Toledo province, which sits in central Spain to the south of Madrid.

The provincial capital Toledo is around 40 miles southwest of the Spanish capital, and the crash involved two trains that were traveling on the line linking Madrid to Seville, which is around a further 200 miles south-west of the city of Toledo.

Toledo province is part of the region of Castilla–La Mancha, of which the city of Toledo is also the capital.

Actual Article Body:
BARCELONA, Spain (AP) — A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 30 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.

The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, said at least 30 people died in the crash and warned that the death toll could rise. He added that at least 80 people were injured.

BUENAS TARDES, Aitor Hernández-Morales here to bring you the latest on how today’s tragedy in Spain is turning political.

NO, CANADA: EU countries have dropped the idea of offering Canada “associate member” status in the 27-member bloc, opting instead for softer language promising “ever closer association.”

TRAIN CRASH LATEST: At least 68 people were killed and 58 injured when two trains collided near Madrid this morning, according to emergency services. Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by an official in the national railway control center in Madrid, who “inexplicably” instructed one high-speed train to proceed along a track where another had stalled.

“We are absolutely devastated,” said Puente, who has been touted as a possible future Socialist Party leader. “We have a safe rail system, comparable to those of other countries in our region.”

Puente declined to say whether he would resign over the tragedy.

**A message from the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Research and Innovation: Ekaterina Zaharieva: Europe has extraordinary talent and ideas. We need to help them go further. Join me at the European Research and Innovation Days on 10–11 November 2026 to discuss how we can connect researchers, innovators and entrepreneurs, support startups and turn discoveries into real benefits for people across Europe.**

GAME OVER? Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s chances of victory in next month’s parliamentary elections already looked like a long shot before today’s train accident. The dream that he’ll be able to continue as PM now looks very unlikely to come true given the Socialist leader’s checkered record on crisis management and improving public services.

Déjà vu: The crash comes less than a year after a train derailment in Adamuz killed 46 people. This raises major questions about the state of Spain’s critical infrastructure and threatens Sánchez’s central pitch to voters: that his government is competent and bettering Spaniards’ everyday lives.

Give it to us straight: “This inevitably upends the campaign and deals a blow to Sánchez,” said a Socialist Party lawmaker who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “It changes the conversation, and naturally the opposition will use it, just as they used the Adamuz accident.” Another anonymous Socialist lawmaker cautioned against writing Sánchez off, noting that a month remains until election day — a lifetime in politics.

Leadership scrutiny: Sánchez will very likely face fresh questions about his leadership. He’s already dealing with corruption scandals involving close allies, and few have forgotten his missteps while handling the mass arrival of migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in July.

Adiós, charm offensive: Sánchez will also probably need to adjust his campaign strategy, at least in the short term. The PM had recently been playing up his charisma in contrast to dour, gaffe-prone rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo and doubling down on his bet to make the election about housing policy. Even Sánchez’s critics had started suggesting his Socialist Party could finish first in the popular vote — though still short of the parliamentary majority needed to govern given the disarray of his potential coalition partners on the left.

Vox doesn’t hold back: Feijóo’s center-right People’s Party, which leads in the polls, has so far limited its response to expressing solidarity with the victims and their families. Far-right Vox leader Santiago Abascal, however, slammed the government. “More deaths. Another tragedy. More anger at the abandonment, ruin and betrayal Spaniards are suffering,” he wrote on X. “I will not rest until this government, which is a criminal organization, is in the dock answering for its crimes.”

BAD TO WORSE: Pessimism is palpable among France’s flailing centrists as they brace for another weekend of protests over conditions in schools and the rising cost of living. “Honestly, I don’t know how we’re going to pull this off. Things are dragging on, and we’re out of ideas,” said one centrist MP granted anonymity to speak candidly.

We’re the problem: Another lawmaker said the government’s failure to stop the violence on the sidelines of the demonstrations that took place on Oct. 17 “is definitely going to kill us. We can no longer be a solution, only a problem.”

Who’s in, who’s out: There are less than six months before the first round of France’s next presidential election, and polls show far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen and far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon have the inside track to take the top two spots and advance to the runoff. Former PMs Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal as well as conservative leader Bruno Retailleau are all bleeding support.

Too many options: “There are too many [candidates],” said France’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot on public radio this morning, echoing calls for centrists, the center-right and conservatives to rally around a single candidate to avoid vote-splitting.

Foreign interference: Barrot and other centrists are trying to seize the narrative about the situation facing France. The FM used his interview to dispel unsubstantiated claims that the violence was linked to immigration, attributing those claims to “interference attempts” from countries including the U.S., Israel, Iran and Russia. But Philippe said in an interview that during the unrest an “overrepresentation of young people from immigrant backgrounds was evident.”

Commissioning a commission: National Assembly President Yaël Braun-Pivet has been attempting to put together a parliamentary commission to investigate the violence that took place over the weekend of Oct. 17 and 18, but even this effort looks imperiled by bickering over which lawmakers get key positions.

BRITISH BUDGET: Chancellor John Healey reduced his fiscal buffer and slapped fresh taxes on banks Wednesday as he announced the first government budget under PM Andy Burnham. Showing his boss is focused on the cost-of-living crisis, Healey promised a £100 energy payment for millions of Brits over the winter, while repeatedly pointing to the war in the Middle East as justification.

PAVLOVIAN RESPONSE: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s top pick for Ukrainian ambassador to the U.S. declined the job in favor of a return to the front line. According to Zelenskyy, former top military commander and current Deputy Head of the President’s Office Pavlo Palisa told his boss: “Get me back to my brigade immediately. I’m not leaving Ukraine.”

MAYDAY: Drones struck a container vessel off the coast of Bulgaria on Wednesday afternoon, said Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov. There is no information yet as to who is responsible, but concerns over attacks on civilian commercial vessels in the region are growing. Bulgaria is also seeking dedicated EU funding in the next long-term budget to help set up a planned Black Sea Maritime Security Hub with Romania.

HEADS UP: As tensions in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean rise, Turkish Defense Minister Yaşar Güler warned Tuesday that Ankara would not compromise on its rights and interests. He also stressed the importance of maintaining open channels of communication with Greece.

BILLET-DOUX: The mayor of Limoges, whose town hall was set ablaze during the unrest in France earlier this month, said this morning he had not been contacted by President Emmanuel Macron since the incident … but had received an e-mail from U.S. Vice President JD Vance, who has turned the unrest in France into a campaign issue ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

FORT TRUMP: Polish President Karol Nawrocki has summoned the country’s top security officials for a Nov. 3 meeting to discuss plans for a permanent U.S. military base, ahead of his meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump at December’s G20 summit in Miami. Dubbed “Fort Trump,” the prospective base would accommodate some 5,000 American troops and their families, at an estimated cost of €3.5 billion.

PATRIOT PRIZE: Poland beat Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host a European servicing center for U.S.-made PAC-3 missiles — the advanced Patriot interceptors used to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles in Ukraine. The facility will allow European militaries to service the sought-after weapons without sending them across the Atlantic.

LET’S TALK: The U.K. will kickstart negotiations with European allies over its joint procurement scheme for their defense industries, after talks collapsed over joining Canada’s defense bank. The Multilateral Defence Mechanism was announced by former PM Keir Starmer’s government in March alongside the Netherlands and Finland. Poland joined in July.

ON THE FENCE: Spain and Slovenia “have not yet decided” if they will compete in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest after boycotting this year’s event over Israel’s participation, the European Broadcasting Union said Wednesday. They have until December to decide. But Ireland, the Netherlands and Iceland will once again boycott the competition.

EXPECT: No planned works or delays on public transit as you head home this evening, according to STIB.

Today’s recommendations are:

READ THIS: “Days of Love and Rage,” an epic portrait of the city of Manbij during the Syrian civil war that took journalist Anand Gopal eight years to complete.

LISTEN TO THIS: A chronicle of What Went Wrong on the set of 1964’s “Dr. Strangelove” and the fear of nuclear war that inspired it.

WATCH THIS: Head to your preferred streamer for the movie that brought us the modern zombie, George A. Romero’s 1968 classic “Night of the Living Dead.”

LEFT IN THE LURCH? HEAD TO THIS: This year’s Pink Screens Film Festival kicks off with an exhibition and concert at LaVallée tonight. More info here.

IMO: The Oxford — or serial — comma serves a purpose and should not be optional punctuation. AP take note. — Leyla Aksu, deputy editor

TALK TO PLAYBOOK: Do you agree? Email us at [email protected] to share your Brussels takes.

TRAIN DREAMS: Spain came to Europe’s high-speed rail revolution relatively late. Italy boasted the continent’s first line in 1977, France in 1981 and Germany a decade on. Spain joined the race in 1992, inaugurating its state-of-the-art AVE service between Madrid and Seville in time for the 500th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’ voyage to the Americas. Pursuing ambitious expansions, it now hosts Europe’s largest network — only China’s is larger. But the Adamuz disaster in January has caused a significant drop in ridership.

Our job is to help them succeed. On 10–11 November 2026, the European Research and Innovation Days will bring these communities together with policymakers and business leaders. We look forward to hearing their ideas on how we can make Europe a better place to do research, build a business and bring new technologies to market. Steering our discussions will be the European Research Area. How can we make it easier for people, knowledge and ideas to move across borders? How can we connect talent with investment and give startups the support they need to grow? Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes | CNN

Scores of people have been killed and around 100 injured after two Spanish trains — carrying about 500 passengers — collided south of Madrid. Follow for live updates.

Actual Article Body:
Live Updates

• Deadly rail crash: Scores of people have been killed and about 100 injured after a high-speed train collided with a stationary train. Spain’s transport minister called it “inexplicable” that a train was allowed to continue its journey despite a red signal being in place.

• ‘People were hurled into the air’: Several witnesses told CNN about the chaotic moment when passengers were thrown airborne during the collision. Rescue operations are still under and the high-speed line linking Madrid with Andalusia remains suspended.

• Third train crash this year: This is the third rail disaster in Spain in 2026. In January, two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz, in southern Spain’s Córdoba province, killing more than 40 people. A commuter train near Barcelona derailed days later.

• Sigue nuestra cobertura en vivo en español

After a host of European leaders offered their condolences for the victims of the deadly train crash in Spain this morning, other international leaders are also expressing their solidarity today.

An erroneous order from a train controller, following a signaling system failure, resulted in Wednesday’s deadly train crash, according to Spain’s transport minister.

Speaking during a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, Óscar Puente said that a computer failure with the main LZB signalling system triggered an automatic stop for all trains in that area, including the Renfe high-speed train and Iryo train involved in the collision.

The control system for Adif, Spain’s railway infrastructure manager, then took command of the system and a decision was made for the Renfe train to continue its journey and the train was authorized to proceed despite a red signal prohibiting movement remaining in place.

The Iryo train remained stationary on the track around 25 kilometers (16 miles) ahead.

The Renfe train was authorized to proceed without any speed restrictions, meaning that between 8:36 a.m. and 8:52 a.m. local time, it traveled approximately 25 kilometers (16 miles) at a speed of about 200 kilometers per hour (124 miles per hour) before colliding with the Iryo train, Puente said.

The transport minister described the crash as “truly implausible” and said that the control center’s decision to allow the Renfe train to resume its journey while the Iryo train was stopped on the track was “inexplicable.”

This post has been updated with additional reporting.

Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said authorities are working hard to identify the cause of today’s deadly train crash in Toledo province, and vowed that any negligence, if identified, will be addressed with “utmost firmness.”

“We are going to get to the bottom of it. And if there has been negligence, it will come to light. And if there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness. Because it is clear that we have suffered two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail in the same year,” he said at a news conference near the site of the crash.

Sánchez added that if Spain must “strengthen safety even further in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so. Because what is unacceptable for a country like Spain is to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have.”

“Therefore, every measure considered appropriate will be taken,” he said.

He also said the cause of the crash was “not for me to say,” but rather for the train network operators and the country’s Independent Commission on Rail Accidents to investigate.

Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is at the scene of the train collision, where he offered his condolences and announced three days of official mourning.

“Today, Spain is in mourning. All of Spain is in mourning,” he said, saying he expressed his “full solidarity” with victims’ families.

“Behind every person who has died today, there are shattered lives, there are broken families. There is also the anguish of those families who still do not know the whereabouts of their loved ones. And, of course, there is a great deal of pain, a great deal of pain that Spanish society as a whole naturally shares.”

At least 68 people have been killed and another 58 have been injured after two trains collided in the Spanish province of Toledo, local officials have said.

Here are some of the latest developments:

CNN’s Magdalena Sofia Vitores Moreno, Benjamin Brown, Sophie Tanno, Vasco Cotovio, Pau Mosquera and Lauren Kent contributed to this reporting.

Emergency crews are working at the site of a deadly train collision in Spain’s Toledo province today, in which at least 64 people were killed and dozens more injured.

Train passengers have told CNN that the moment of the crash was “very chaotic” and people were immediately thrown out of their seats and on top of one another inside the train carriages.

Authorities have moved at least one bus full of passengers who do not have serious injuries away from the site. Several passengers being bussed away had minor injuries, including cuts on their faces and around their eyes, and what appeared to be bloody noses. Many people also had blood on their hands and arms.

“There was terrible communication. No one could leave the trains for 10 minutes after the crash, we didn’t know what was happening,” said one passenger, Rey, who declined to give his last name.

He said he and his family, who were on the way to a vacation in Seville, are OK but also “desperate to go.” More busses have arrived on the scene now to move additional passengers away from the area.

Another passenger, Yoander, 25, told CNN: “I was sleeping, and when I woke up I was already crashing into the seats in front of me.”

“I hit my face and my leg,” he said. “I’m in pain, but there are people that need more help than I do.”

The deadly train crash in Spain’s Toledo province has some similarities with a train disaster in Córdoba province that killed more than 40 people earlier this year.

Both train collisions happened along the same high-speed rail route that runs between the capital, Madrid, and Seville, about 300 miles south.

The Toledo crash happened about 130 miles from the site of January’s train disaster near Adamuz, in Córdoba province. Following Wednesday’s crash, authorities have suspended that high-speed line linking the Madrid region with Andalusia.

Both train accidents also involved the collision of two high-speed trains, although one of the trains on Wednesday was not travelling at high speed at the time of the crash.

Spanish emergency authorities have not yet announced a precise cause of Wednesday’s crash, but they have disclosed some details. The local Castilla-La Mancha 112 emergency services told CNN they received a report of a collision at 8.45 a.m. local time. According to the reports, a train owned by the company Iryo was stationary or traveling at low speed when it was struck by a high-speed AVE train operated by Spain’s national railway company Renfe.

It appears the crash on Wednesday was a rear-end collision, authorities at the scene told CNN. The train crash earlier this year involved one train derailing and crossing onto an adjacent track, according to Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE.

For context: Spain’s train drivers’ union, Semaf, has previously raised concerns about high speeds causing vibrations and subsequent wear and tear along high-speed railway lines, a source from the union told CNN in January, in the aftermath of the crash near Adamuz.

In August 2025, the union sent a letter to the national railway operator, Adif, asking for a reduction in the maximum speed on all high-speed train lines from 300 kmph to 250 kmph, after some stretches were vibrating and placing stress on the infrastructure, the source said.

CNN’s Pau Mosquera, Tim Lister and Sophie Tanno contributed to this report.

Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will travel to Urda, the town closest to the site of the train crash, the country’s government said in a post on X.

While in Urda, Sanchez will  “back the works of the emergency teams and bring support to the affected and their families,” the government said.

“The priority is to tend to the victims and provide the best coordination among different administrations,” the social media post continued.

There has been an outpouring of grief from neighboring European leaders today, after two trains collided in the Spanish province of Toledo, killing dozens of people.

Leaders from the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Belgium, Germany, Ukraine, The Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, Norway, Finland, the Czech Republic, Lithuania, Latvia, Romania, Estonia, Croatia, North Macedonia, Slovakia, Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Andorra also expressed their sympathies.

CNN’s James Frater, Duarte Mendonça, Sharon Braithwaite and Magdalena Vitores Moreno contributed to this reporting.

Correction: An earlier version of this post misstated the title of French President Emmanuel Macron.

At least 64 people have now been confirmed killed in a deadly train collision in Spain this morning, a spokesperson for the regional Castilla-La Mancha government said.

The spokesperson told CNN that this number is expected to rise further as emergency workers continue to work at the scene.

The death toll from today’s train crash in the Spanish province of Toledo has now risen to at least 32, according to Emiliano García-Page, the president of the regional Castilla-La Mancha government.

García-Page shared the latest update when speaking to Spanish national broadcaster Radio Nacional de España.

Previously, authorities had said that at least 30 people had been killed and around 100 injured in the collision.

The Spanish Civil Guard announced that they have opened four offices in different cities of Spain in order to swiftly identify the victims of the crash.

A spokesperson of institution has said they will also take DNA samples of the relatives to bring a quick response. “We are calling all close relatives to get to this offices and speed up the identification process,” the spokesperson said.

The offices are in the Civil Guard zones of Madrid, Andalusia, Cordoba and Toledo.

CNN’s Pau Mosquera has been reporting from Urda, a town roughly five miles from the site of today’s deadly train crash.

Dozens of ambulances and emergency service vehicles have been streaming into the town’s sports centre, where Red Cross workers are treating the injured.

One of the survivors recounted how she was thrown from her seat as the crash’s impact sent her flying into the air. She was grateful for the care provided to her by the emergency staff in Urda.

The scene at the site of the crash is frantic as a serious rescue operation is underway, according to CNN’s team on the ground in Toledo province.

Dozens of fire trucks, ambulances and police cars are here. At least three helicopters are also at the crash site to assist with operations. Multiple ambulances have come and gone from the cordoned-off area.

Meanwhile, emergency responders are combing through the rubble of some of the heavily damaged carriages of the train operated by Iryo. Several carriages of the state-owned Renfe high-speed train are tilted on their side after coming off the rails.

The Spanish civil guard has set up multiple tents for what amounts to a huge emergency response.

Authorities have moved a bus full of passengers who do not have serious injuries away from the site, and some those passengers told CNN they are now being taken to their original destination of Sevilla.

Passengers described a chaotic scene when their train hit another train on the tracks.

Those being bussed away from the crash site included citizens of multiple nationalities, including Spain, Brazil and elsewhere. Staff from the US Embassy in Spain are also at the site.

A woman traveling on one of the trains involved in a deadly collision Wednesday morning has described “awful” scenes as people were thrown into the air.

Patricia was sitting in the third carriage of the AVE high speed train, operated by Renfe, Spain’s national railway company, when it collided with a train owned by the company Iryo.

Speaking to CNN, Patricia told how her train had been stopped for around 20 minutes before the accident, with an announcement explaining there was a lot of traffic. “After that we departed, and maybe not after even three minutes, there was a crash,” she said.

Patricia said the crash seemed to last a long time.

“Some people were hurled into the air. Not me. I was on the left side so I suppose that’s why I wasn’t hurled in the air, but it was awful.”She continued, “Some of the train structure got into our train, in our carriage, and our carriage wasn’t even the worst.”

The Castilla-La Mancha regional government has called for blood donations following today’s train crash.

“Donate blood,” reads a post on X. “Today your solidarity is very important.”

The post calls for donations in Alcázar de San Juan, Ciudad Real and Toledo.

At least 30 people have been killed and around a hundred injured in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo this morning, according to a local government official and emergency services. The incident is the third rail disaster in Spain this year.

CNN’s Pau Mosquera, Sophie Tanno, Magdalena Sofia Vitores Moreno and Lauren Kent contributed to this reporting.

At least 30 people have been killed after two trains collided in Spain this morning, according to a local government official.

The spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government told CNN that the death toll is likely to rise.

This post has been updated with additional developments.

Today’s train crash occurred in Toledo province, which sits in central Spain to the south of Madrid.

The provincial capital Toledo is around 40 miles southwest of the Spanish capital, and the crash involved two trains that were traveling on the line linking Madrid to Seville, which is around a further 200 miles south-west of the city of Toledo.

Toledo province is part of the region of Castilla–La Mancha, of which the city of Toledo is also the capital.
